title: Second opinion: perfect just may reach moral certainty excluding fear, like historical human faith
source_text: XVII. Secunda sententia quae circa hanc quaestionem locum habet in Schola Romana, non docet quidem teste Bellarmino, justos habere posse de propria gratia certitudinem fidei divinae; tamen affirmat posse, imo etiam solere praesertim homines perfectos, pro hujus vitae statu, ad eam securitatem venire, ut nullam habeant de sua justificatione formidinem: plane ad eum modum quo credimus sine ulla haesitatione, & formidine deceptionis, Caesarem imperasse in Italia, Alexandrum in Graecia; Ciceronem Oratorem, Livium Historicum, Virgilium Poetam fuisse; Constantinopolim esse Urbem in Thracia, & Antiochiam in Syria, quamvis neutram viderimus. Quae certitudo illa est quae proprie moralis dicitur, & distinguitur a conjecturali.
pass_a_gloss: The second opinion which has place on this question in the Roman School does not indeed teach, according to Bellarmine, that the just can have concerning their own grace the certainty of divine faith; yet it affirms that they can, and even that especially perfect people usually for the state of this life come to such security that they have no fear concerning their justification—plainly in the way we believe without any hesitation or fear of deception that Caesar ruled in Italy, Alexander in Greece; that Cicero was an orator, Livy a historian, Virgil a poet; that Constantinople is a city in Thrace and Antioch in Syria, although we have seen neither. Which certainty is that which is properly called moral, and is distinguished from the conjectural.
pass_b_english: The second Roman view denies divine-faith certainty of grace but allows moral certainty without fear.
It likens that security to our firm historical belief about Caesar, Virgil, or distant cities never seen.
